student.title: Literacy Lab: Respectful Attribution in Research

content.text: Part A: Audit Your Research for Attribution (W.6.8)
(15 minutes)
Rehearse and Refine
Directions:

Choose one sentence from your synthesis claim and corroborated statement that includes information you learned from a print or digital source. If working digitally, use comments, highlighting, or a shared document tool to mark what needs attribution before revising. Use the 3-Column Chart to copy the sentence, identify what needs attribution, and revise it so it names the specific culture or community and the source clearly.
Part B: Revise and Reflect on Responsible Sharing (W.6.8)
(15 minutes)
Turn and Talk
What part of your sentence is your own conclusion, and what part came from a source?
How can you revise your sentence so it names the specific culture or community more respectfully?
Directions:

Use your revised sentence from Part A to write a four-to-five-sentence research reflection in your journal. Your reflection should 1) state your synthesis idea, 2) attribute at least one source-based detail clearly, and 3) answer the question: What do we owe communities when we use their knowledge?
Model:

Multiple myths explain the movement of the sun and moon as the work of two powerful supernatural beings, which describe who controls their paths and why. According to the Inuit story of Malina and Anningan retold in [text title] and the Greek myth about Helios and Selene in [text title], the sun and moon are siblings that cross the sky. When I share this information, I owe those communities and authors clear attribution because the stories come from real traditions, not from my imagination. Clear citation, including title and author, also helps my reader check where my information came from.

Share your paragraph with your partner orally or through a shared digital document, if available. Listen for whether the draft names a specific culture or community, includes an attribution phrase, and explains why citation matters. Partner A, read first. Partner B, give one glow and one grow. Then switch.
How did your partner show respect for source creators and communities in their revision?
What sentence in your partner’s draft best answers the question “What do we owe those communities when we use their knowledge?”
Quick Write
Directions:
Respond to both reflection prompts in three to four sentences. Use at least two specific details from your revised synthesis or source list.
What changes did you make today to use information more responsibly?
What are your next steps before you share this research in your essay or seminar?
Display the following three-sentence opening script and read it aloud:
Say:

In the previous lesson, we used notes from more than one source to write synthesis claims about how different cultures explain the natural world. Today, we are asking what responsibilities come with sharing those stories and ideas, especially when we use the Internet, digital sources, or classroom publishing tools to share information from specific cultures and traditions. This matters because your final writing and seminar work should not only be accurate, but also respectful and trustworthy.
Have students take out their Research Notes organizer and synthesis claim from Lesson 22.
Turn-and-Talk
Teacher Guidance: Partners should each have their Lesson 22 artifacts in front of them. The goal is to move students from “I finished my research” to “I am responsible for how I share it.”
Say these Directions:

Look at your synthesis claim and source notes. With your partner, name one idea in your writing that came from a source and one thing you think a responsible researcher should do before sharing that idea with others.
Ask:
What information in your synthesis and corroboration came from other people’s knowledge or storytelling, and what responsibility do you have when you use it?

My comparison of Greek and Māori stories came from research sources, not just from my own thinking. That means I should name the specific cultures, make sure I paraphrase in my own words, and include where I found the information so readers know I am not pretending the idea came from me.
Say:
Partner A, share first. Partner B, listen for the source-based idea and the responsibility. Then switch.
Teacher Tip

Myths and traditional stories come from real cultural traditions, and some are connected to living religions and community knowledge today. Remind students that studying mythology as literature does not require adopting any belief system and that respectful sharing means naming specific cultures or communities rather than using broad labels like “people believed” or “Native Americans believed.”
Support students in orally naming the difference between their own conclusion and an idea they learned from a source.
Prompt students to point physically to one phrase in their synthesis claim that came from a source before they speak.
If a student uses a broad label, invite a revision by asking for the most specific culture or community name available in their notes.
You said, “I got this from the internet” — we can say: “I learned this idea from a source in my research notes, so I need to attribute it clearly.”
That idea connects to attribution because naming the source shows where the information came from.
One idea in my synthesis that came from a source is ___.
I should name ___ specifically because ___.
Before I share this information, I need to ___.
Allow students a brief turn-and-talk discussion to clarify ideas, including use of a shared home language, before sharing with the whole group.
Invite students to connect this idea to how names, authorship, or family stories matter in their own communities.
If students describe only the topic and not the sourced idea → Prompt: “Point to one sentence in your claim. Which part did you learn from reading?”
If students confuse a culture name with a continent or broad group label → Prompt: “Can you replace that broad label with the specific community named in your source?”
Student names one specific idea that came from a source, rather than speaking only in general topic terms.
Student revises broad language toward a more precise culture or community name.
Connection to Today's Learning
Students have identified that research creates responsibility. Next, they will learn a clear process for checking whether their writing credits sources and communities respectfully.
Reconnect students to their Lesson 22 synthesis artifacts and surface the ethical question behind attribution: “What responsibilities do researchers have when sharing cultural knowledge?”
Rehearse and Refine
Use the same teacher-maintained model topic from Lesson 22:
how myths explain the movement of the sun and moon across the sky
. Model with a short sample synthesis claim and corroboration that is too general first. Then revise it with specific attribution.
Display the following teacher model:

Weak version: Many cultures made stories to explain the movement of the sun across the sky. The story of Malina and Anningan and the story of Helios and Selene say the sun moves because of divine figures, but for different reasons.

Stronger version: Multiple cultures have myths explaining the movement of the sun and moon as the work of two powerful supernatural beings, describing who controls their paths and why. In both the story of Malina and Anningan and the story of Helios and Selene, the sun and moon are siblings that cross the sky. However, they do so for different reasons.
Explain: The stronger version shows that these stories both explain a natural phenomenon, but I still need to credit the cultures they came from and cite the source itself.
Say these Directions:

When checking our synthesis statements, we are going to use a simple three-part check. First, identify the sourced idea. Second, name the specific culture or community instead of using a broad label. Third, add attribution so a reader can tell where the information came from.
Say:

When I look at my first sentence, I notice that it sounds like the information belongs to me, even though I learned it from sources. A responsible researcher stops and asks, “Which part is my conclusion, and which part came from reading?” My conclusion is that both stories explain the sun, but the details about Malina and Helios came from sources, so they need attribution. I also notice that saying “both cultures” is too vague. Respectful attribution means I name the specific culture or community when I can, and I also give source information, including the author, title, and source name. This is part of responsible digital citizenship because writers often use technology and the Internet to gather, revise, and share information with others. That helps me avoid plagiarism, but it also shows respect for the people and traditions connected to the story.
Ask:
In both the weak and stronger model statements, what is missing that a responsible researcher needs to include?
Both are missing the source and the specific culture names. The stronger one names both cultures, but it does not tell the reader where the information came from.
Ask:
Why is respectful attribution more than just “not getting in trouble”?

Respectful attribution matters because these stories come from real communities and traditions. Citing the source shows honesty, and naming the culture specifically shows respect for whose knowledge I am using.
Support students in using precise research language to distinguish sourced information from their own conclusions.
Model the sentence frame orally first. Then have students rehearse it with a partner before applying it to their own notes.
When students say “this is mine,” clarify whether they mean the wording is theirs or the idea is theirs.
You said, “This part is mine” — we can say: “This conclusion is my synthesis, but the detail itself came from a source and still needs attribution.”
You said, “I should say where it’s from” — we can say: “I should attribute the idea by naming the specific culture and source.”
This detail came from ___, so I need to attribute it.
Instead of saying ___, I can name the specific culture or community: ___.
My conclusion is ___, but my evidence came from ___.
Allow students to rehearse a sentence in everyday language first. Then help them shift it into academic language.
Encourage students to use what they already know about the importance of naming family, community, or place accurately as a bridge to academic attribution.
If students think paraphrased ideas do not need citation → Prompt: “Did the idea begin with you, or did you learn it from a source? If it came from a source, cite it.”
If students name only the source but not the culture or community → Prompt: “What specific people or tradition does this source discuss?”
Student distinguishes between a personal conclusion and a sourced detail using precise language.
Student uses a specific culture or community name instead of an overgeneralized label.
Check for Understanding (W.6.8)

Look at your own synthesis claim and corroboration. Underline the part that is your conclusion, identify the part that came from a source, and explain what kinds of attribution are needed to name the specific culture or community and the source.

“The myths of several cultures explain earthquakes by saying they are caused by the sudden movement of a powerful force, which suggests that people used stories to make sudden and frightening natural events feel more understandable. In the stories about Rūaumoko and Namazu, the ground shakes because something moves below people’s feet, but the force behind that motion is imagined differently in each culture.” I named the specific stories, but now I need to add the cultures they come from and the sources where I read them.
Modeling
If needed, prompt students to begin with: “In my statement, I named ____ but I still need to give credit to ___.”
Connection to Today's Learning
Now that students have practiced the three-part check with a model, they are ready to audit and revise their own research writing.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with:
Distinguishing Sourced Ideas from Their Own Conclusions:
Have students say the idea aloud without looking at the source. Then prompt, “Did you learn that from reading or from your own thinking? If it came from reading, it needs attribution.”
Naming Specific Cultures and Communities:
Direct students back to their notes and highlight where a source names a people, place, or tradition.
Written Expression:
Allow students to orally rehearse their revision with a partner or use speech-to-text before writing it into the organizer.
Ready for extension

Have students explain how a vague label changes the meaning of a sentence and why the more specific wording is stronger and more respectful. Have students revise two sentences instead of one, including one sentence that compares sources and one that explains a difference between them.

teacher.title: Literacy Lab: Respectful Attribution in Research

content.text: Teach how respectful attribution works in grade 6 research by distinguishing personal conclusions from sourced ideas and by naming specific cultures, communities, and sources.
Part A: Audit Your Research for Attribution (W.6.8)
(15 minutes)
Rehearse and Refine

Students work independently first and then briefly compare revisions with a partner. The goal is to audit one or two sentences from Lesson 22 and revise them for clearer attribution and cultural specificity.
Say these Directions:

Choose one sentence from your synthesis claim and corroborated statement that includes information you learned from a print or digital source. If working digitally, use comments, highlighting, or a shared document tool to mark what needs attribution before revising. Use the 3-Column Chart to copy the sentence, identify what needs attribution, and revise it so it names the specific culture or community and the source clearly.
Teach
Say:

Start with your original model sentence: “In both the story of Malina and Anningan and the story of Helios and Selene, the sun and moon are siblings that cross the sky.” Copy it into the first column so you can analyze it. In the second column, identify what’s missing — specifically, the cultures and source titles — and add that information. In the third column, revise the sentence to include those details, for example: “According to the Inuit story of Malina and Anningan retold in [text title] and the Greek myth of Helios in [text title], both cultures explain the sun’s movement as the actions of deities.”
This version is still a draft, but it’s stronger because it adds specificity and clearly attributes the ideas to sources. Apply this same revision strategy to your own sentence.
Provide students this completed sample row if needed:
Original sentence
What needs attribution?
Respectful revision
In both the story of Malina and Anningan and the story of Helios and Selene, the sun and moon are siblings that cross the sky.
Specific culture names, source information
Based on my notes, I know that:
The source on the Inuit story is [title, author’s name, source type].
The source on the Greek myth is [title, author’s name, source type].
According to the Inuit story of Malina and Anningan retold in [text title] and the Greek myth about Helios and Selene in [text title], the sun and moon are siblings that cross the sky.
Ask:
What part of your sentence is your own conclusion, and what part came from a source?

My conclusion is that both stories explain the same natural phenomenon by saying it is caused by something moving underground. The details about Rūaumoko moving below the earth and the Japanese legend about Namazu came from my sources, so those details need attribution, including the author and title.
Ask:
How can you revise your sentence so it names the specific culture or community more respectfully?

I can replace “people believed” with “In a Māori story about Rūaumoko” or “In the Japanese Namazu legend.” That is more respectful because it tells the reader exactly whose tradition I am talking about.
Support students in using explanatory language to identify missing attribution and revise source-based writing with precision.
Prompt students to use the phrase “This detail came from …” before they attempt a written revision.
If a student has multiple sources in one sentence, help them slow down and revise one source-based idea at a time.
You said, “I need to fix this part” — we can say: “I need to revise this part so the attribution is clear and specific.”
That idea connects to respectful sourcing because the revision tells the reader whose tradition and which source the detail comes from.
This detail came from ___, so I need to name ___.
My sentence is too general because ___.
A more respectful revision would be ___.
Invite students to compare how names and labels matter in their own lives, such as family names, community names, or place names.
Allow students to talk through a revision first in a shared home language and then write the academic English version.
If students keep writing “some cultures” or “people believed” → Prompt: “Look back at your notes. Who specifically is named there?”
If students can identify the problem but cannot revise the sentence → Prompt: “Start with: ‘In my source ___, the story from ___ explains ___.’”
Student identifies one exact phrase in the sentence that needs attribution or greater specificity.
Student revises vague wording into a sentence that names a source and a specific culture or community.
Checklist
Activity:
Attribution Audit in 3-Column Chart
Circulate and provide real-time feedback based on the following observable language behaviors:
Target 1 (Source Use): Student distinguishes between a synthesis conclusion and a sourced detail.
Target 2 (Specificity): Student replaces broad labels with a specific culture or community name when available in notes.
Target 3 (Attribution): Student adds enough source information for a reader to understand where the idea came from, including title, author (if available), and type of source.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with:
Revising Vague Wording
: Offer the stem, “In my source ___ about ___ tradition, the story explains ___.”
Finding Where a Detail Came from:
Have students trace the sentence back to the matching note on their Research Notes organizer before revising.
Organizing Written Revisions:
Allow students to orally record the revised sentence or use speech-to-text and then copy the final version into the chart.
Ready for extension
Ask students to revise a second sentence that compares two sources and uses a comparative transition, such as
both, unlike
, or
however.
Ask students to explain how respectful attribution also helps a reader check credibility.
Part B: Revise and Reflect on Responsible Sharing (W.6.8)
(15 minutes)
Turn-and-Talk

Teacher Guidance: Students now use their revised attribution to write a complete, cited synthesis statement and a reflection on the changes they made. They should write first and then share with a partner for quick feedback on respect, clarity, and traceability.
Say:

As I draft, I want my writing to do two jobs at once. First, it should state my conclusion clearly. Second, it should show that I understand my responsibility as a researcher. I begin with my synthesis claim. Then I add source-based details using attribution phrases like “According to my source …” or “In my research on ...” After that, I include one sentence that explains why this matters, not just for school rules, but for respect and trust. When I reread, I check that my paragraph cites the source, names the culture or community, and makes my responsibility clear.
Say these Directions:

Use your revised sentence from Part A to write a 4–5-sentence research reflection in your journal. Your reflection should 1) state your synthesis idea, 2) attribute at least one source-based detail clearly, and 3) answer the question: “What do we owe communities when we use their knowledge?”
Display the following writing model if needed for support and guidance:

Multiple cultures have myths explaining the movement of the sun and moon as the work of two powerful supernatural beings, describing who controls their paths and why. According to the Inuit story of Malina and Anningan retold in [text title] and the Greek myth about Helios and Selene in [text title], the sun and moon are siblings that cross the sky. When I share this information, I owe those communities and authors clear attribution because the stories come from real traditions, not from my imagination. Clear citation, including title and author, also helps my reader check where my information came from.
Say:

Share your paragraph with your partner orally or through a shared digital document, if available. Listen for whether the draft names a specific culture or community, includes an attribution phrase, and explains why citation matters. Partner A, read first. Partner B, give one glow and one grow. Then switch.
Ask:
How did your partner show respect for source creators and communities in their revision?
My partner showed respect by naming the Cherokee story specifically instead of saying “Native Americans believed” and by adding where the information came from so the reader can trace the source.
Ask:
What sentence in your partner’s draft best answers the question, “What do we owe those communities when we use their knowledge?”

The strongest sentence in the draft says, “I owe those communities accurate naming and clear attribution because these stories belong to real traditions and should not be treated like random information I found online.”
Teacher Tip

If students use overly broad labels for Indigenous, regional, or religious traditions, pause the class and model a respectful correction. Emphasize that part of digital citizenship is not flattening many communities into one category when a source gives a more precise name.
Support students in composing a short written explanation that combines source attribution with ethical reflection.
Encourage students to link ethics and evidence with connector, such as
because, so
, and
this matters because.
If students write only about school rules, prompt them to expand toward respect, trust, and community knowledge.
You said, “I have to cite so I don’t get in trouble” — we can say: “I cite sources because responsible sharing shows respect and helps readers verify my information.”
That idea connects to digital citizenship because using information ethically means both attributing it and thinking about who is affected.
According to ___, ___.
This matters because ___.
When I share this information, I owe ___ to the community because ___.
Invite students to draw on personal experiences with being credited correctly for ideas, art, or stories, as a bridge to academic attribution.
Allow students to draft orally with a partner before writing independently.
If students list source information without explaining why it matters → Prompt: “Add a
because
sentence that explains the responsibility behind the citation.”
If students explain the ethics but do not actually attribute a source → Prompt: “Show your reader one place where the information came from.”
Student writes a paragraph that includes both a correctly cited attribution and an explanation of responsibility.
Student avoids broad generalizations and instead names a specific source and community when available.
Pulse Check (W.6.8)
Which statement best shows understanding of respectful attribution and responsible use of cultural knowledge?
Many people long ago made stories about the sun, and I learned that from research.
Incorrect: This choice stays too general. It hints that research happened, but it does not name a source or a specific culture or community.
I changed some words from a website about myths, so now the idea is mine.
Incorrect: This distractor reflects the misconception that changing a few words makes a sourced idea original. Paraphrased ideas still need attribution.
According to the Māori story of Māui and the sun, Māui slows the sun to make the days longer, so I should cite the source when I share that detail.
Correct: This answer names the source-based idea, the specific tradition, and the responsibility to cite it clearly.
The internet says that cultures believed lots of different things, which proves my paragraph is accurate.
Incorrect: This distractor reflects the misconception that a vague reference to “the Internet” counts as attribution or evidence. It does not help a reader verify the source.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with:
Writing the Reflection Paragraph:
Provide a three-part outline in their journal: “My synthesis idea is ___ / According to my source ___ / This matters because ___.”
Explaining What They Owe Communities:
Prompt with, “What would respectful sharing look like if this were your family’s story?”
Drafting Independently:
Allow students to record an oral version first or use speech-to-text and then revise for clarity and attribution.
Ready for extension

Ask students to include a second attributed detail from another source and use a comparative transition to connect the two. Ask students to add one sentence answering the larger question, “Who controls what we know, and how does citation push back against confusion or erasure?”
Part A: Audit Your Research for Attribution (W.6.8)
Students will review one synthesis claim with corroboration at a time to identify what must be attributed and then revise for specificity and respect.
Part B: Revise and Reflect on Responsible Sharing (W.6.8)
Students will draft a short revised response that includes attribution and a reflection on what they owe communities and sources when they use their knowledge.
Say these Directions:

Today you revised your research so it is more accurate, more respectful, and easier for a reader to trust. In your final project, that same habit will help you explain myths clearly and ethically when you compare stories across cultures. Think about one specific change you made today and how it will strengthen your writing or speaking later in the unit.
Quickwrite
Say these Directions:
Respond to both reflection prompts in 3–4 sentences. Use at least two specific details from your revised synthesis or source list.
What changes did you make today to use information more responsibly?

Today I changed my writing so it named the Māori source specifically instead of saying “some cultures.” I also added an attribution phrase to show that the detail about Māui came from research, not from my own imagination. These changes make my paragraph more respectful and more trustworthy.
What are your next steps before you share this research in your essay or seminar?

My next step is to check my other source and make sure I have the author, title, and source name written down. I also want to revise one more sentence so it explains why both stories matter without making the cultures sound the same.
Support students in reflecting on changes to their language and in naming clear next steps for responsible source use.
Encourage students to name an exact revision move instead of writing only “I fixed my paragraph.”
Prompt students to use next-step language that is specific and doable.
You said, “I made it better” — we can say: “I revised one sentence to add specific attribution and a clearer culture name.”
That idea connects to next steps because good researchers keep checking for accuracy and respect before sharing.
One change I made today was ___.
This improved my writing because ___.
My next step is to ___ so my research is more ___.
Allow students to rehearse their reflection with a partner before writing.
Encourage students to connect responsible school research to respectful sharing in everyday digital spaces.
If students write only one vague sentence → Prompt: “Name the exact word or phrase you changed.”
If students struggle to identify a next step → Prompt: “What is one source detail you still need to check before sharing your work?”
Student names a specific revision move made during the lesson.
Student states a clear next step tied to attribution, citation, or respectful cultural naming.
Scoring Rubric
Criterion
1 — Developing
2 — Approaching
3 — Meets
W.6.8 — Reflecting on ethical use of source-based information
Response gives a general statement about research but does not name a specific change or next step.
Response names either a specific change or a next step, but details are limited or not tied clearly to responsible source use.
Response names a specific change and a clear next step, using details from the student’s revised synthesis or source list to explain responsible attribution.
W.6.4 — Producing a clear written reflection
Response is hard to follow or incomplete.
Response is mostly clear but may be repetitive or loosely organized.
Response is clear and organized and uses appropriate academic language to explain the student’s thinking.
Students will reflect on changes they made to use sources more responsibly and set next steps for sharing research in the performance task.

Review one print or digital source you may use in your performance task. In your Journal or digital notes, record the author, title, and source name, and write one sentence explaining why that source should be credited clearly before you share your research.

data.subject: ELA

standards.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of three pages in a single sitting.

Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess the credibility of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and providing basic bibliographic information for sources.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of three pages in a single sitting.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.
Express inferences and conclusions drawn based on close reading of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia using a variety of precise academic verbs (e.g., indicates that, influences).
Express inferences and conclusions drawn based on close reading of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia using some frequently used verbs (e.g., shows that, based on).
Express inferences and conclusions drawn based on close reading of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia using a variety of verbs (e.g., suggests that, leads to).

vocabulary.definition: naming where an idea, story, or detail came from
source information that helps a reader find the original text
restate an idea in your own words and sentence structure
using someone else’s words or ideas without giving credit
ideas, stories, and understandings that come from a community or tradition

content.text: How do stories from different cultures explore danger, courage, or the unknown?
